walkthroughs.body_html:
Research Methods — a core area of A-Level Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Research Methods brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Research Methods.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A square frame of known area used to estimate plant abundance is a:
options: Quadrat
Transect
Pooter
Anemometer

mcqs.q: To study how vegetation changes from a path into woodland, the best technique is a:
options: Transect
Single random quadrat
Questionnaire
One-off observation

mcqs.q: Choosing sample sites using random coordinates mainly helps to reduce:
options: Bias
The area studied
The number of species
Rainfall

mcqs.q: Taking repeat readings and calculating a mean mainly improves a method's:
options: Reliability
Bias
Cost
Danger

mcqs.q: Does a single quadrat give a reliable estimate of plant abundance?
options: Yes; one quadrat is enough to represent the whole area.
No; several quadrats are needed and a mean calculated to give a representative estimate.
Quadrats can only be used on animals, not plants.
Random sampling means picking the easiest spots to reach.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between random and systematic sampling?
options: Random sampling chooses sites by chance; systematic sampling takes them at regular intervals, such as along a transect.
Random sampling means picking the easiest spots to reach.
Reliability only matters for questionnaires.
They are two names for the same method.

mcqs.q: Does a reliable result always mean a valid one?
options: Reliability only matters for questionnaires.
Yes; reliable and valid mean exactly the same thing.
No; a method can give consistent (reliable) results yet still not measure what it claims (invalid).
Random sampling means picking the easiest spots to reach.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Quadrat”?
options: Choosing sample locations by chance, for example using random coordinates, to avoid bias and make results representative of the area.
The extent to which a method actually measures what it claims to, depending on appropriate controls and accurate, relevant techniques.
A square frame of known area placed on the ground to count or estimate the abundance of plants or slow-moving animals within it.
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results if repeated, improved by taking repeat readings and calculating a mean.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Validity”?
options: A square frame of known area placed on the ground to count or estimate the abundance of plants or slow-moving animals within it.
A line laid across a habitat along which samples are taken at intervals to study how species change along a gradient such as distance from a shore.
The extent to which a method actually measures what it claims to, depending on appropriate controls and accurate, relevant techniques.
Choosing sample locations by chance, for example using random coordinates, to avoid bias and make results representative of the area.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Reliability”?
options: The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results if repeated, improved by taking repeat readings and calculating a mean.
Choosing sample locations by chance, for example using random coordinates, to avoid bias and make results representative of the area.
A line laid across a habitat along which samples are taken at intervals to study how species change along a gradient such as distance from a shore.
Selecting a representative subset of an area or population to study, since it is rarely possible to measure every organism or location.

The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results if repeated, improved by taking repeat readings and calculating a mean.
Selecting a representative subset of an area or population to study, since it is rarely possible to measure every organism or location.
A square frame of known area placed on the ground to count or estimate the abundance of plants or slow-moving animals within it.
